On the morning of the Varalakshmi puja, Ishita arranged the kalasha in the front room of their house in Hassan and waited. Aditi, home from college in Mysuru, came down in jeans with a book.
'You're not getting ready?'
'I'll help cook, Amma. I don't want to do the puja this year.'
Ishita's hands stopped on the mango leaves. Her sister-in-law would arrive at ten. What would she say? And under that, a colder thought: had she failed her daughter somewhere?
She almost snapped. Instead she wiped her hands, sat on the step and said, 'Tell me what's changed. I'm not angry. I want to understand.'
Aditi sat beside her, surprised. They talked for twenty minutes about books, a friend's funeral, questions with no easy answers. Then Aditi grated coconut, and Ishita lit the lamp alone, with less heaviness than she had expected.

qa.a: Aditi had come home from college in Mysuru.

qa.a: She worried what her sister-in-law would say, and feared she had failed her daughter somewhere.

qa.q: What would have changed if Ishita had snapped at Aditi?

At the village temple festival, the drums were so loud Shankar could feel them in his teeth. He stood at the edge of the crowd with his cousin Lokesh, arms folded.
'You used to carry the lamp,' Lokesh said.
'I used to be terrified,' Shankar said. 'Remember Periyappa telling us that if we missed a single festival, the crops would fail and it would be our fault? I was nine. I lay awake over it.'
His voice came out sharper than he meant. A woman in front turned round.
'So now you're angry,' Lokesh said, not unkindly.
'Now I don't know what I am. Angry, mostly. Some days just empty.' Shankar watched the chariot lurch forward. 'Everyone expects me to either come back or announce I'm done. I can't do either yet.'
Lokesh handed him a cup of panakam and didn't argue.

qa.a: He said the crops would fail and it would be their fault.

qa.a: It reveals anger at having been frightened as a child, still raw enough to spill out louder than he meant.

The call to prayer drifted across the rooftops of Kadıköy as Zeynep sat on the balcony with cold tea. For most of her life that sound had meant something: stop, wash, turn toward something bigger. Now it only meant that it was evening.
She wasn't angry, the way some friends were about their upbringing. She just felt a quiet hollow where the meaning used to be, like a room after the furniture has gone.
Pablo, her flatmate, came out with a blanket. 'You've been out here an hour.'
'I keep waiting to feel something when I hear it,' she said. 'Either way. Relief, or missing it. Nothing comes.'
'Maybe it doesn't have to come yet,' Pablo said.
Zeynep pulled the blanket round her shoulders and listened to the last notes fade.

On Tuesdays Hana took the late train home from the lab with two books in her bag: a copy of the Dhammapada her grandmother had given her, and a thick book on the philosophy of mind that her colleague Anders, a cheerful sceptic, had lent her.
She read one, then the other, pencil in hand, writing questions in the margins. Does a self exist? Does it matter for how I treat people?
On Thursdays she sat with an old monk at the small centre in Nørrebro, who answered many questions with 'Try it and see.' On Fridays she argued with Anders over coffee.
Neither had convinced her. That no longer frightened her. She had started a notebook titled 'Things I don't know yet', and it was growing. She liked it better than the years of not asking.

Three years after she had stopped going to the village temple, Parul climbed the stone steps again on the morning of the Nanda Devi fair. Her cousin Harish raised his eyebrows but said nothing.
She didn't do everything she used to. She skipped the long list of vows her aunts recited. She didn't tie a thread for a wish. She simply stood in the cold courtyard, hands folded, and gave thanks for her mother's recovery and for the mountains she had missed in Delhi.
'So you're back?' Harish asked on the way down.
'Not the way I was,' Parul said. 'Then I prayed because I was scared not to. Now it's because I want to. I'm keeping the parts that feel true.'

In Guadalajara, Clara still set the table for Sunday lunch at her abuela Rosa's house, still lit a candle for her grandfather on his day, still volunteered at the Saturday food bank the parish ran. She no longer went to Mass.
It had taken her three years of reading, arguing and long walks to say it plainly: she didn't believe in God. Saying it hadn't made her feel lost, as she had feared. It had made her feel honest.
'And yet you still come to the food bank,' Rosa said, passing the rice.
'I still believe people shouldn't go hungry,' Clara said. 'That part didn't go anywhere.'
Rosa looked at her for a long moment, then nodded. 'Your grandfather would have liked that answer.'
